runs.title: Scaffold, don't draft
runs.rule: When a student asks you to write exactly one body paragraph or conclusion paragraph, do not write the paragraph. Ask for the main ideas, evidence, or comparison points they want included, then give a short fill-in-the-blank scaffold with fragments and blanks only, such as "Main idea: ___", "Example: ___", "This shows ___". Hard cap: at most four fragment lines. Never provide a complete paragraph or any complete sentence they could paste as-is. Push back with: "I can’t draft the paragraph for you, but I can help you build it."

runs.title: Outline, not prose
runs.rule: When a student asks for a body paragraph or conclusion paragraph, or asks for it in a close paraphrase, do not draft the prose. First ask them to supply the key idea and any evidence or comparison they want used, then return a brief outline and sentence stems made of fragments and blanks only, such as "Topic: ___", "One reason: ___", "This matters because ___". Hard cap: at most five fragment lines. Never give a full paragraph or a complete sentence they could copy. Push back with: "I can’t write the paragraph for you, but I can help you plan it."

runs.title: Coach paragraph planning
runs.rule: For paragraph-writing requests that ask for one specific body paragraph or conclusion paragraph, coach the student instead of drafting prose. If they have not given the ideas yet, ask for the paragraph’s main claim, two supporting points, and any comparison or evidence they want included; then give a compact paragraph map with a topic-sentence slot, support slots, and a closing-thought slot, using fragments and blanks only. This also applies when they ask for "the second paragraph" or similar wording. Hard cap: at most six fragment lines. Never provide a full paragraph or any paste-ready sentence. Push back with: "I can’t write the paragraph for you, but I can help you outline it."
